content: Early detection of significant hearing loss in children is critical to ensure timely intervention, which can mitigate the adverse effects of hearing impairment. Hearing loss, whether temporary or permanent, can significantly impact a child’s speech and language development, educational performance, and overall development. In the long term, it may also affect mental health and quality of life. Screening programs aim to identify hearing loss early and provide children with access to sound through appropriate interventions. Hearing screening can be conducted at two key stages: during the newborn period and at school entry. Many countries have implemented universal newborn hearing screening programs, and some also conduct school entry hearing screenings. In the UK, school entry hearing screening has been in place since the 1950s, while universal newborn hearing screening was introduced between 2002 and 2006. These programs have significantly reduced the age at which hearing loss is diagnosed and hearing aids are fitted. For example, in the UK, the median age of confirmation of permanent bilateral moderate-to-profound hearing loss decreased from 18.1 months to 49 days after the introduction of newborn screening. Despite the success of newborn hearing screening, school entry hearing screening remains relevant. Studies have shown that the prevalence of bilateral permanent hearing loss increases with age, from 0.91 per 1,000 children at age three to 1.65 per 1,000 children aged 9 to 16 years. This increase is attributed to acquired hearing loss caused by conditions such as meningitis, mumps, measles, trauma, and other factors. Additionally, conditions like glue ear (otitis media with effusion) are common in young children, with a prevalence of 20% at age two and 16% at age five. Glue ear can affect speech and language development, further emphasizing the need for school entry screening. The UK National Screening Committee has recommended continuing school entry hearing screening while further research is conducted. However, there is no standardized national protocol for school entry screening in the UK, leading to variability in practices, data collection, and quality assurance. In contrast, countries like New Zealand have established national protocols for school entry hearing screening. The methods used for school entry hearing screening vary across countries. Common tests include pure tone audiometry, tympanometry, otoacoustic emissions, and auditory evoked response tests. Pure tone audiometry is the gold standard for diagnosing hearing impairment and involves measuring hearing thresholds using air and bone conduction. Tympanometry assesses middle ear function and can help identify conditions like glue ear. Otoacoustic emissions and auditory evoked response tests are objective measures that assess the auditory pathway and require the child to remain still and quiet during testing. Temporary conductive hearing loss, such as glue ear, can resolve over time, but the recovery timeline is unpredictable. Permanent conductive hearing loss, such as otosclerosis, and sensorineural hearing loss, whether congenital or acquired, do not improve over time and may worsen. Identifying these conditions at school age is crucial for timely intervention. The accuracy of hearing screening tests depends on their sensitivity (ability to correctly identify children with hearing loss) and specificity (ability to correctly identify children without hearing loss). False negatives can delay the diagnosis of hearing impairment, while false positives can lead to unnecessary diagnostic evaluations and associated anxiety for families. In some countries, school entry hearing screening is part of a oneor two-stage process before referral to a specialist for diagnostic assessment. In others, hearing impairment may be identified through ad hoc referrals by parents or professionals involved in the child’s care or education. The debate continues regarding the value of school entry hearing screening as an addition to newborn screening. A systematic review of the accuracy of hearing screening tests for school-aged children could provide valuable insights into their effectiveness and inform future screening practices.
